Family Health

A purple or bruised penis: when to seek care

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A purple patch on the penis has several possible explanations, from bleeding under the skin to a skin condition or a circulation problem. Colour alone cannot establish the cause. How suddenly it appeared, whether there was an injury and whether you have pain, swelling or urinary symptoms are more useful clues.

Check for emergency symptoms first

Go to emergency care if an injury to an erect penis causes sudden pain, rapid swelling or bruising, especially with a cracking sound or immediate loss of the erection. This can be a penile fracture: a tear in the covering of the erectile tissue, despite there being no bone. It usually needs urgent surgical treatment.

A foreskin trapped behind the head of the penis and unable to move forward is another emergency, called paraphimosis. Swelling and a dark or purple colour can reflect restricted circulation. Do not wait for it to settle or repeatedly force the skin.

Seek immediate care for severe pain, rapidly worsening swelling, inability to pass urine, significant bleeding or a penis that becomes dark and numb. An erection lasting about four hours also needs emergency treatment; painful prolonged erections may need help sooner. Embarrassment should not delay assessment.

Bruising and collections of blood

A bruise forms when small blood vessels leak into nearby tissue. Friction, a knock or a pinch can cause a local mark, which may change colour as it heals. A haematoma is a collection of blood that may produce more noticeable swelling. You cannot reliably judge the depth or seriousness just by whether it feels soft or firm.

Avoid further friction or sexual activity if the area is sore, and arrange prompt review if the cause is uncertain, the patch spreads, swelling increases or symptoms persist. A significant injury should be assessed even if pain begins to ease. Do not massage or puncture a swelling.

Tell the clinician about blood-thinning medicines and any bruises elsewhere, nosebleeds or blood in urine or stool. Do not stop an anticoagulant on your own. The team may need to assess a bleeding tendency as well as the local injury.

A zipper pinch, friction during sex or masturbation, or a sports injury are examples of possible trauma. A small clearly explained bruise may fade gradually, but an enlarging mark, persistent tenderness or a more substantial injury needs review rather than a promise that it will heal within a fixed number of weeks.

Purple spots can have other causes

Purpura describes bleeding into the skin; it is not one specific disease. It can result from damage to small vessels, inflammation, platelet problems or other conditions. A new unexplained cluster of spots warrants medical assessment, especially with bleeding elsewhere or feeling unwell.

Some medication reactions cause a sharply defined red or violet patch that returns in the same place after exposure to the same medicine. This is called a fixed drug eruption and can affect the genitals. Mention all recent medicines, including non-prescription painkillers, but do not deliberately take another dose to test the connection.

A widespread painful rash, blistering or peeling, particularly with mouth or eye sores after a new medicine, needs emergency care. These features can occur in a rare serious reaction such as Stevens–Johnson syndrome. Bring your medication list or packaging to the assessment.

Nutritional deficiency, medicines or a bleeding or clotting disorder can contribute to unexplained bruising in some people. Mention abdominal or joint pain, fever, new fatigue and bruises beyond the genital area, rather than focusing only on the colour of one patch.

Skin disease and infection need different treatments

Lichen sclerosus can cause pale or scarred patches, fragile skin, bruising, tearing or a tightening foreskin. It is not a sexually transmitted infection. A dermatologist or urologist can assess it and recommend treatment; stronger steroid ointments require a specific plan, and some people need surgery for complications.

Genital ulcers or blisters may also be caused by infections, including herpes or syphilis. Other conditions can look similar, so a visual guess is unreliable. A sexual-health clinic can arrange suitable tests and explain treatment, partner advice and when sexual contact is safe.

Do not apply leftover antibiotics, antifungal creams or potent steroids simply because an online photograph looks similar. The wrong treatment may irritate the skin or delay the diagnosis. An ulcer, lump or patch that does not heal also deserves examination.

Herpes or syphilis can cause genital sores with pain, itching, burning or urinary discomfort, although syphilis sores may be painless and infections can have few symptoms. Syphilis can be cured with appropriate treatment; herpes can be managed with antiviral treatment but is not eradicated by a short course.

What to expect at an appointment

The clinician will ask when the change started, whether it is progressing, about recent injury or sexual contact, and about medicines and symptoms elsewhere. They may examine the skin, foreskin and surrounding area and check circulation or urinary function.

Depending on the findings, testing may include a swab, blood or urine tests, or imaging for an injury. Not everyone needs an ultrasound. Ask what diagnosis is most likely, how to care for the area and which changes mean you should return sooner.

If you are uncomfortable discussing the problem, you can begin with a simple description: a new purple patch, when it appeared and whether it hurts. You can also request a chaperone or ask the service about clinician preferences where available.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

NHS identifies a trapped foreskin and prolonged painful erection as urgent conditions; major injury with sudden bruising and swelling also needs emergency assessment.

CDC advises testing for genital ulcers because appearance alone is unreliable. Dermatology guidance distinguishes purpura, drug reactions and lichen sclerosus from infection.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you describe when the colour changed, any injury and recent medicines. A clinician must assess circulation, injury and skin findings.

When to seek help

Sudden bruising after an erection injury, a dark numb penis, trapped foreskin, inability to urinate or prolonged erection needs emergency care. A blistering widespread rash with mouth or eye sores is also an emergency.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • New discolouration cannot be diagnosed from colour alone.
  • Sudden bruising after an erection injury or a trapped foreskin is an emergency.
  • Unexplained spots, ulcers or persistent changes need medical assessment.
  • Treatment depends on the cause, not on matching an online photograph.

Frequently asked questions

Does purple always mean an STI?

No. Bruising, circulation problems, skin disease and drug reactions are other possibilities.

Can I wait if an injury stops hurting?

Not if there was a significant injury, rapid bruising, swelling or loss of an erection. A serious tissue injury can still need urgent care.

Should I use steroid cream?

Only when a clinician has diagnosed a condition for which that treatment is appropriate and given instructions.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
